note: Summaries are written by Claude from each paper's abstract. Items marked 'title only' had no abstract available — open the paper before relying on them.

items.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term

summary.method: From the title: a study of how to discretize the momentum convection term so it stays consistent with the VOF interface transport (22 pages; code released).
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: This is your proposal's second requirement, conservative transport across density jumps, from the isoAdvector/plicRDF author. Compare its mass–momentum consistency fix with how your solver advects momentum next to the air film at a 1000:1 density ratio.

items.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part I: The gravity force term
items.authors: J. Roenby, K. Missios, K. Møller et al.

summary.method: From the title: how the gravity body-force term should be discretized consistently with the interface and pressure so it does not create spurious velocities (code released).
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Gravity/pressure imbalance at a density jump is a classic source of parasitic currents in water-entry runs; useful for your spurious-current section and for OpenFOAM validation choices.

items.title: Solver-consistent learned curvature for algebraic volume-of-fluid simulations of rising bubbles: symmetry-preserving networks, closed-loop data aggregation and a posteriori benchmarks

summary.method: From the title: a neural-network curvature estimator for algebraic VOF that respects symmetries and is trained in closed loop with the solver, then tested a posteriori on rising bubbles.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: The closest new relative of PLIC-Net: the 'closed-loop data aggregation' idea (training on states the coupled solver actually produces) is a direct answer to the a-priori vs a-posteriori gap you will face when PLIC-Net runs inside a full simulation.

items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.method: The authors keep the sign in a modified formulation and test both versions in volume-of-fluid simulations of droplet impact and bubble coalescence.
summary.problem: The common Kistler dynamic contact-angle implementation uses the magnitude of the capillary number, so it loses the sign that distinguishes advancing from receding contact lines.
summary.result: The magnitude-based model mispredicts droplet recoil and suppresses bubble detachment, while the corrected model captures both.

items.title: Correcting a capillary-number sign pitfall in Kistler dynamic contact-angle modeling
items.why: Directly relevant to the contact angle on a moving solid in your proposal: during water entry the contact line on the sphere both advances and recedes, so check whether your Kistler/Cox–Voinov implementation keeps the sign of Ca.

items.authors: H. Wu, H. Qi, Y. Zhang et al.

summary.method: Water-entry experiments over a range of cylinder temperatures, entry speeds and diameters, with cavity shapes reconstructed from high-speed images using a Logvinovich-type model.
summary.problem: How does heating a cylinder change the air cavity it opens when it enters water at high speed?
summary.result: A hotter cylinder generally made the cavity grow longer along its axis and delayed pinch-off, while maximum cavity diameter and pinch-off depth changed little (the abstract gives no numbers).

items.title: Experimental study of thermally induced cavity evolution and periodic layered cavities during water entry of heated cylinders
items.why: Heating changes the gas layer and effective wetting at the moving solid, so this is a fresh experimental data set for your proposal's 'contact angle on a moving solid' and 'sub-cell gas layer' requirements, and a possible validation target for the air film in your solver.

summary.method: The closed-form inverse square root of the homogeneous operator is folded into the finite element factors so the preconditioned operator has subnormalization one, and QSVT block-encodes its inverse.
summary.problem: Quantum linear solvers slow down under mesh refinement because the finite element stiffness matrix of a two-phase conduction problem has a condition number that grows quadratically with elements per side.
summary.result: On three periodic cells with up to 10^6 unknowns the condition number stayed mesh-independent, and Qiskit state-vector runs on 4×4 and 8×8 meshes matched the classical solution within the polynomial tolerance.

items.title: A Preconditioned Quantum Linear Solver for Periodic Two-Phase Heat Conduction with Mesh-Independent Condition Number
items.why: This is the exact obstacle in your quantum pressure solver study and Poisson condition-number note: a two-phase coefficient jump plus mesh refinement drives kappa up. Check whether the homogeneous-operator preconditioning idea survives a 1000:1 density ratio in the variable-density pressure Poisson equation.

summary.method: From the title: a quadratic (curved) interface reconstruction for VOF, paired with a geometric way to extend velocity off the interface.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.title: Parametrised-Quadratic Interface Reconstruction and Geometric Velocity Extension in the Volume-of-Fluid Framework
items.why: A direct step beyond PLIC: worth comparing against PLIC-Net and your curvature / spurious-current tests, since curved reconstruction is the usual answer to PLIC's curvature error.

items.title: Stokes flow in a wedge with a moving contact point: well-posedness with a fixed contact angle and Navier slip
items.authors: M. V. Gnann, H. Knüpfer, K. M. Lam et al.

summary.method: From the title: a mathematical proof that Stokes flow near a moving contact point is well-posed when the contact angle is fixed and the wall has Navier slip (172 pages).
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Gives rigorous backing for the slip-regularized contact line your review discusses under Cox–Voinov and mesh dependence; a good citation when you justify a Navier-slip condition on the moving solid.

items.title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
items.authors: G. Cassoni, F. Gennari, J. Serafini et al.

summary.method: From the title: a reduced-order sloshing model that includes contact-line hysteresis and a curvature correction, for tanks in low gravity.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: A compact way to represent pinning and hysteresis energy loss; worth a look for the hysteresis part of your contact-line section and as a contrast to full CFD treatments.

items.title: Wake-Powered Spreading of Encapsulated Drops Impacting Under Liquid

summary.problem: Drop-spreading models assume the drop's own kinetic energy drives spreading, which fails when the wall sits under another liquid.
summary.method: Millimetric oil drops, bare or coated with a thin silicone-oil shell, were dropped onto a glass wall under water and analysed with a two-stage energy balance.
summary.result: The drops spread to more than twice their diameter, and over 90% of the spreading energy came from the wake rather than the drop itself.

items.why: A clean example of the surrounding fluid (not the impactor) controlling wetting during impact, which parallels how the air layer shapes the contact line on a body entering water.

items.title: PANDA-D: Interface-free determination of two dynamic contact angles from molecular-density and center-of-mass profiles
items.authors: G. K. Vandyshev, G. S. Gorkaev, N. D. Kondratyuk

summary.problem: Measuring contact angles in molecular dynamics depends on arbitrary density thresholds, and a density profile alone cannot tell which meniscus is advancing and which is receding.
summary.method: The density profile and layer-by-layer centre-of-mass displacement are fitted together with a circular-meniscus model, giving both angles without extracting an interface.
summary.result: On synthetic cases with known angles the error was 0.29° RMS, and estimates agreed with independent circle fits to 0.84° RMS over 167 angles.

items.why: Advancing-vs-receding separation is exactly the issue on a moving solid; a source of microscale dynamic-angle data for calibrating the contact-angle rule in your proposal.

items.title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
items.authors: K. Bennema ten Brinke, R. Ramesh, D. Orij et al.

summary.problem: High-fidelity simulation of swarms of deformable bubbles is expensive, and the dynamics are nonlinear and chaotic.
summary.method: A neural surrogate forecasts bubble paths and interface shapes together in a spherical-harmonic representation, using generative flow matching to predict whole future windows at once.
summary.result: It reproduces key flow statistics and runs several orders of magnitude faster than the DNS solver it learns from.

items.why: A different ML route from PLIC-Net: learn compact shape coefficients instead of cell-level reconstruction. Good framing material for the ML part of a job talk.

items.title: A variational multiscale rotational pressure-correction method for incompressible flows with open boundaries

summary.method: From the title: a rotational pressure-correction (projection) scheme combined with variational multiscale stabilization, aimed at open-boundary flows.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Rotational projection reduces the pressure boundary-layer error; a reference point for the projection-method part of your Poisson note, though it is single-phase.
